title: Scikit-Learn Reasoning
blurb: Reason about the estimator protocol, data leakage, pipelines and metrics the way a code reviewer does — before anything runs.

cells.title: The estimator protocol: fit learns, the rest read
cells.body:
Every scikit-learn estimator obeys one protocol, and knowing it lets you simulate code without running it. fit is the only method that learns: it mutates the estimator, writing attributes with a trailing underscore (mean_, coef_, classes_), and it returns self so calls can chain. transform, predict and score are stateless readers: they reuse the learned attributes, never modify them, and demand that fit ran first — otherwise they raise NotFittedError.

The reasoning habit: whenever you see an estimator in review code, ask 'which state does this call read or write, and has that state been learned yet?' Almost every classic pipeline bug — refitting on test data, predicting before fitting, transforming with the wrong scaler — falls out of that one question.

demo.code:
class ScalerSim:
    """Mimics the sklearn estimator protocol."""
    def fit(self, rows):
        cols = list(zip(*rows))
        self.mean_ = [sum(c) / len(c) for c in cols]
        return self                      # fit() returns self
    def transform(self, rows):
        return [[v - m for v, m in zip(row, self.mean_)] for row in rows]

s = ScalerSim()
print('fit returns self:', s.fit([[1.0], [3.0], [5.0]]) is s)
print('learned mean_:', s.mean_)
print('transform reuses it:', s.transform([[1.0], [5.0]]))

cells.title: Fit on train, transform on test
cells.body:
Preprocessing is part of the model, and it must be learned from training data only. A StandardScaler stores a mean and a scale; the contract is: fit on X_train (learn the statistics), then transform on both X_train and X_test (reuse them). Calling fit — or fit_transform — on the test set re-learns the statistics from the test set.

That is data leakage: the evaluation stops measuring 'how does the model handle unseen data, preprocessed the way it was trained' and starts measuring 'how does it handle test data preprocessed with knowledge of itself'. Scores come out optimistic, and nothing crashes — which is exactly why this bug is invisible unless you look for it. Keep the picture of two different mean values in your head and you will spot the bug instantly in review.

demo.code:
train = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
test = [10.0, 20.0, 30.0]

train_mean = sum(train) / len(train)
print('correct: test - TRAIN mean =', [round(v - train_mean, 1) for v in test])

test_mean = sum(test) / len(test)
print('leaky:   test - TEST  mean =', [round(v - test_mean, 1) for v in test])
print('the model was trained on the first kind of numbers, not the second')

cells.title: Reading a confusion matrix
cells.body:
A confusion matrix is a small counting table, and the whole skill is which cells feed which formula. With sklearn's convention — rows are the TRUE label, columns are the PREDICTED label — the diagonal holds correct predictions. For the positive class (usually 1): TP is the bottom-right cell, FP the top-right (predicted 1, truly 0), and FN the bottom-left (truly 1, predicted 0).

Then precision = TP / (TP + FP) reads down the predicted-positive column: 'of everything I flagged, how much was real?'. Recall = TP / (TP + FN) reads across the true-positive row: 'of everything real, how much did I catch?'. Both are class-specific — computing them for class 0 uses the other diagonal cell — and neither is accuracy, which is just (TP + TN) / total.

demo.code:
# sklearn convention: rows = TRUE label, columns = PREDICTED label
cm = [[7, 3],
      [2, 8]]
TP, FN = cm[1][1], cm[1][0]
FP, TN = cm[0][1], cm[0][0]
print('true 1s:', TP + FN, ' predicted 1s:', TP + FP)
print('precision = TP/(TP+FP) =', TP, '/', TP + FP, '=', round(TP / (TP + FP), 3))
print('recall    = TP/(TP+FN) =', TP, '/', TP + FN, '=', round(TP / (TP + FN), 3))

exercise.title: Predict: predict before fit
exercise.statement: First protocol check — you are reviewing a script that trains a classifier, and you spot a predict call suspiciously early in the file. No coding: execute the snippet in your head and predict what it prints.
exercise.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

clf = LogisticRegression()

try:
    clf.predict([[1.5, 2.0], [0.5, -1.0]])
    print('got predictions')
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)
exercise.explain: Every supervised estimator guards predict with a fitted-check: fit is the only method that learns state (it writes trailing-underscore attributes like coef_ and classes_), and predict refuses to run before that state exists — it raises NotFittedError, so the snippet prints that class name. B assumes the model lazily trains itself on the fly; sklearn never does that. C is a memory of very old versions, which crashed with a raw AttributeError on the missing coef_ — modern sklearn raises the specific error instead. D is close but wrong as printed output: NotFittedError really is a subclass of ValueError (so except ValueError would catch it), but type(e).__name__ prints the most specific class, which is NotFittedError.

exercise.title: Pick the reason: fit_transform on test data
exercise.statement: Now a code-review question about reasoning, not output. The flagged line below is a real data-leakage bug. Four explanations are proposed — pick the one that states the correct reason it is a bug.
exercise.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit(X_train).transform(X_train)

# the reviewer flags THIS line:
X_test_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_test)    # BUG

model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
print(model.score(X_test_scaled, y_test))        # too optimistic
options: A. It is a bug because fit_transform computes a different formula than fit followed by transform, so the test features end up on a different scale than the training features.

B. It is a bug because fit_transform re-learns the mean and standard deviation from the TEST set, so the test features are standardized with statistics the model never saw — test information leaks into the evaluation and the score turns optimistic. The fix is scaler.transform(X_test), which reuses the training statistics.
C. It is a bug because fit_transform is deprecated for scalers in modern scikit-learn and is only kept for backward compatibility.
D. It is a bug because the scaler was already fitted on X_train — calling fit again on an already-fitted estimator raises an error.
exercise.explain: The method is not the problem — for StandardScaler, fit_transform(X) computes exactly fit(X).transform(X). The problem is which data learns the statistics: fitting on X_test overwrites mean_ and scale_ (remember, fit mutates state) with test-set values, so the evaluation quietly measures the model on data centered by the test set's own statistics. That is leakage, and it makes scores optimistic — nothing crashes, which is why reviewers hunt for it. A has the math wrong (the two calls are equivalent); C is false — there is no deprecation; D is false — refitting an estimator is perfectly legal, and that permissiveness is precisely what makes this bug possible. The fix: scaler.transform(X_test).

exercise.title: Predict: features entering the model
exercise.statement: Shape math under a pipeline. The preprocessor scales two numeric columns and one-hot encodes one categorical column with exactly three possible values; a logistic regression sits at the end of the pipeline. Predict what the final print outputs.
exercise.code:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

# X_train columns: 'age', 'income' (numeric) and 'color',
# where color takes exactly 3 values: red / green / blue.
# y_train is binary (two classes).
pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ('num', StandardScaler(), ['age', 'income']),
    ('cat', OneHotEncoder(), ['color']),
])
pipe = Pipeline([('pre', pre), ('clf', LogisticRegression())])
pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(pipe.named_steps['clf'].coef_.shape)
exercise.explain: Do the feature arithmetic transformer by transformer. StandardScaler rescales each column in place: 2 numeric columns in, 2 columns out — it changes values, never counts. OneHotEncoder with default settings emits one binary column per category seen during fit: 3 categories, so 3 columns (it only drops a column if you explicitly pass drop='first'). The ColumnTransformer then concatenates the blocks side by side: 2 + 3 = 5 features entering the classifier. For the rows: this is a binary problem, and binary LogisticRegression stores a single coefficient row, so coef_.shape is (1, 5). A counts the raw DataFrame columns; B assumes one-hot drops a category by default; D assumes one coefficient row per class — that only happens for multiclass problems with more than two classes.

exercise.title: Predict: precision and recall from the matrix
exercise.statement: Finish with metric arithmetic — the kind you should be able to do on a whiteboard. Given this confusion matrix for a binary classifier, predict the precision and recall of the positive class (1), rounded to two decimals.
exercise.code:
# Confusion matrix produced by sklearn's
# confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred) for classes [0, 1].
# sklearn convention:
#   rows    = TRUE label
#   columns = PREDICTED label
#
#                 pred 0   pred 1
#   true 0     [    40       10   ]
#   true 1     [     5       45   ]

cm = [[40, 10],
      [ 5, 45]]
exercise.explain: First label the cells for the positive class 1: TP = cm[1][1] = 45 (truly 1, predicted 1), FP = cm[0][1] = 10 (truly 0 but flagged), FN = cm[1][0] = 5 (truly 1 but missed), TN = 40. Then the arithmetic: precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 45 / (45 + 10) = 45/55 ≈ 0.82 — of the 55 flagged samples, 45 were real. Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 45 / (45 + 5) = 45/50 = 0.90 — of the 50 real positives, 45 were caught. A swaps the two denominators: precision reads down the predicted-positive column, recall across the true-positive row. C is the same pair of formulas applied to class 0 instead: 40/45 ≈ 0.89 and 40/50 = 0.80. D is neither — 0.85 is the accuracy, (40 + 45) / 100, which answers a different question entirely.
